As North Texans break early voting records, Tarrant County becomes an election battleground by Penelope Rivera | KERA News, Fort Worth Report November 2, 2026

As North Texans break early voting records, Tarrant County becomes an election battleground

by Penelope Rivera | KERA News, Fort Worth Report
November 2, 2026

Friday was the last day to vote early, and Texas, including North Texas, saw record breaking numbers in voter turnout.

More than 19 million Texans were registered to vote this year, and 7.4 million of those cast their ballots across the state between Oct. 19 through Oct. 30.

There were 1.8 million people that headed to the polls across North Texas: Dallas County saw 607,886 voters, Collin County had 374,250, Denton County received 319,081, and Tarrant County saw 571,950 ballots, according to each county’s websites.

Tarrant County, long considered a political battleground for Texas, had the highest turnout in county history for early voting in a midterm cycle.

It’s considered a purple county as it mirrors the increased polarization between the two political parties, leaving people watching closely, said Matthew Wilson, political science professor from Southern Methodist University.

As Tarrant County is the largest Republican-led county across the nation, Wilson told KERA News it’s become a closer, more hotly contested race than in the past.

“It gets a disproportionate amount of attention in terms of local races because it’s the last urban county in the state where Republicans are still robustly competitive,” Wilson said. “They would really like to hold on to that, and Democrats would like to take that last Republican urban bastion.”

Early voting sites saw lengthy lines and hours-long wait times across the county’s 47 locations.

At the White Settlement Public Library, voters like Brenda Bedrosian were looking at wait times up to an hour.

Bedrosian, 76, said she initially left after seeing how long the line was Wednesday afternoon — but came back after deciding her vote would be worth the wait.

“It’s a privilege to vote, it’s a privilege to have a voice,” Bedrosian said. “It’s what we want to vote for, whoever we are, whatever values we have.”

Tarrant County Commissioners in August approved cutting 92 voting sites on Election Day — almost a third of all locations — and three sites for early voting, despite population growth.

Charles Barker, another early voter, said he wanted to beat any potential longer lines on Election Day.

Barker, 56, said several statewide races like the U.S. Senate and state comptroller were top of mind for him, but also wants to see less polarization when it comes to county governance.

“I like to think I’ve voted for the person,” Barker said. “If you can articulate what your agenda is, how you want to implement the agenda and what you believe the impact is, and you can articulate that then I’m willing to give you an opportunity.”

Tarrant County has multiple seats on the ballot this year, including county judge, district attorney, and Precincts 2 and 4.

What’s at stake?

It’s the first election since Republican county commissioners approved an unusual, mid-decade redistricting last year that heavily impacted Precincts 1 and 2 — both seated by the two Democratic commissioners on the court.

County Judge Tim O’Hare and commissioners Matt Krause and Manny Ramirez were vocal about their hopes of turning the commissioners court more GOP friendly with the new map.

But the new map also encouraged Democratic voters to go out and cast their ballots, said Allison Campolo, Chair of the Tarrant County Democratic Party.

“People who have never been engaged in politics, people who have never wanted to vote, volunteer or donate turned out because of the county commissioner redistricting the political racist gerrymandering that went on,” Campolo said.

The redistricting also encouraged Democratic commissioner Alisa Simmons to announce her bid for county judge. Incumbent Republican Tim O’Hare is her opponent seeking reelection.

Tarrant County Republican Party Chairman Tim Davis did not respond to requests for an interview, but told CBS News he’s “confident” Republican voters will surpass Democratic voters.

“Yeah, I’m confident,” Davis told CBS. “I think that’s what we’re seeing. They’re kind of running out of votes.”

The county judge race, along with the other local races, has earned Tarrant County a lot of attention, according to Wilson.

“The respective candidates have a history of feuding with each other,” Wilson said. “And that has added a kind of dimension of local intrigue and interest in addition to what’s going on at the statewide level.”

Tarrant County’s races are a test of the political dynamic that will determine whether Republicans can maintain dominance or Democrats will be able to flip it blue.

Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3.
